newsitem.title: JAPAN: SKI JUMPING-JUMPERS TEST FIRST OLYMPIC WIND NET.
newsitem.headline: SKI JUMPING-JUMPERS TEST FIRST OLYMPIC WIND NET.

text.p: Ski jumpers preparing for a World Cup event took their practice leaps on Thursday from behind the protection of crane-mounted nets which officials hope will shield competitors from shifting winds at the Nagano Winter Olympics next year.
The three synthetic nets, each measuring 20 metres by 20 metres, were hoisted on Tuesday on the southern side of the stadium where jumpers will compete for Olympic gold medals next February.
Wind nets were first erected last year at similarly exposed jump sites in Lahti, Finland and Holmenkollen, Norway, but have never been used for the Olympics.

"Its a test net," said Torbjorn Yggeseth, chairman of the International Ski Federation's (FIS) jump committee. "We will try to find the best position for this net so that we will have the best protection during the Olympics next year."
When the optimum angle and height have been determined, permanent masts will replace the cranes, Yggeseth added.
The FIS, who were concerned about the variable winds at the Hakuba stadium, asked organisers last year to provide a provisional net for the World Cup and a permanent net for the Olympics.
Variable winds create unfair conditions for competitors, who are judged on distance and jumping style.
The nets, which stretch from the judges' tower to the take-off area, were hardly needed on Thursday as it was sunny and calm after two days of heavy snowfall.
Four rounds of practice jumps, instead of the scheduled three rounds, were held at the coachs' request after training was cancelled on Wednesday because of the weather.
Forty-six jumpers from 13 countries are scheduled to compete on the large hill on Saturday and then on the normal hill on Sunday.
The FIS also requested that lights be installed in the Hakuba stadium so that Olympic competitions could be held in the evening if bad weather forced cancellation of morning events, said Yggeseth.
The request was turned down because of cost and environmental concerns, said Toru Ushikoshi, chief advisor to the Nagano organising committee.
